notes:
Task and constraints: Find the minimum number of character deletions needed to make word1 and word2 identical.
Idea: Compute the longest common subsequence length using a two-dimensional DP table.
Technique and why it applies: Matching characters extend the best common subsequence of the two preceding prefixes. When they differ, the code takes the better LCS after dropping one character from either word. The minimum deletions equal m+n-2*LCS.
Invariant: a[i][j] is the LCS length for the first i characters of word1 and first j characters of word2.
Edge cases: Empty strings produce a zero-sized border and return the other string's length. The code builds the table manually but correctly initializes its borders to zero.
Complexity: The nested loops take O(mn) time and the full table uses O(mn) space.

Task and constraints: Compute the fewest deletions needed to make two strings equal.
Idea: Use the LCS recurrence with only two rows of dynamic-programming storage.
Technique and why it applies: For each pair of characters, the current row uses values from the previous row and the current row's left neighbor. Matching characters can extend the diagonal LCS; the final deletion count is m+n minus twice the LCS length.
Invariant: dp[(i+1)%2][j+1] stores the LCS for prefixes ending at word1[i] and word2[j] after the current update.
Edge cases: Empty strings return the length of the other string because the table remains zero. The modulo row index reuses storage across iterations.
Complexity: The DP takes O(mn) time and O(n) auxiliary space for two rows, matching the author labels.

Task and constraints: Return the boundary trees of the convex hull around a set of points, including points lying along hull edges.
Idea: Sort and deduplicate points, then build lower and upper monotonic chains using cross products.
Technique and why it applies: cross determines the turn orientation of three points. The code pops only clockwise turns, retaining collinear boundary points, and combines the two chains without their repeated endpoints.
Invariant: Each partial chain follows the sorted points and excludes turns that bend clockwise under the chosen strict comparison.
Edge cases: Empty or single-point inputs return directly. The modified final slice attempts to handle repeated endpoints, but all-collinear and small point sets should be tested because `result[1]` and the truncation can produce duplicates or omit boundary points.
Complexity: Sorting and chain construction take O(n log n) time and O(n) space for the chains and deduplicated point list.

Task and constraints: Validate a code snippet with properly nested uppercase tags and correctly delimited CDATA sections.
Idea: Scan character by character, using a stack to match opening and closing tag names and special handling for CDATA.
Technique and why it applies: Opening tags push names; closing tags must match the stack top. CDATA is accepted only inside an open tag and skipped through the next ]]> marker. Plain text is legal only while the stack is nonempty.
Invariant: stk contains the unmatched open tags at the current scan position.
Edge cases: Empty code fails at code[0] and code[-1], though the problem requires a nonempty snippet. Tag names must contain 1–9 uppercase letters; malformed or unterminated CDATA returns False.
Complexity: The scan advances through the input and each tag is pushed and popped once, giving O(n) time and O(n) stack space.

Task and constraints: Determine whether a snippet forms one valid root tag containing valid nested tags, text, and CDATA.
Idea: Parse recursively with helpers for text, CDATA, tag names, and complete tag bodies.
Technique and why it applies: validTag parses an opening name, parses its content recursively, and then requires the matching closing sequence. validText advances to the next '<', while validCData skips content to the first ']]>'.
Invariant: Each successful validTag returns the index immediately after a complete matched tag.
Edge cases: The final result requires the root parser to consume the entire string, preventing trailing text outside the root. The recursive parser can reach depth O(n) for deeply nested tags.
Complexity: Each character is examined by parsing helpers, giving O(n) time and O(n) recursion stack space, consistent with the labels.

Task and constraints: Evaluate a sequence of signed fraction additions and subtractions and return the reduced result as numerator/denominator.
Idea: Normalize minus signs, parse fractions, compute a common denominator, sum scaled numerators, then divide by a gcd.
Technique and why it applies: Each fraction numerator is scaled by lcm/denominator so all terms share one denominator. The gcd reduction produces the final simplest fraction string.
Invariant: result is the accumulated numerator over the common denominator lcm before reduction.
Edge cases: The code uses floating-point division in lcm and in numerator scaling, which can lose precision for larger values. get_gcd uses recursive subtraction and can be slow for relatively prime large operands. Empty expressions are not handled.
Complexity: Parsing is O(n), but recursive lcm/gcd arithmetic may require many steps; worst-case time can be large relative to numeric magnitudes. Storage is O(n) for parsed numerator and denominator lists.

Task and constraints: Decide whether four points form a square, including rotated squares.
Idea: Compute all six pairwise distances, sort them, and check for four equal shorter distances and two equal longer distances.
Technique and why it applies: A square has four equal sides and two equal diagonals, with the diagonal longer than the side. However, this implementation uses Manhattan distance rather than Euclidean squared distance, so the expected side/diagonal relationship is not reliably preserved for arbitrary orientations.
Invariant: d contains the six pairwise Manhattan distances in sorted order.
Edge cases: The check rejects coincident points through d[0]>0. The Manhattan metric can create false positives or negatives for rotated or non-axis-aligned configurations; use of this metric is the main correctness concern.
Complexity: Six distances and a fixed-size sort take O(1) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Check whether four points form a square in two-dimensional space.
Idea: Compute all six squared Euclidean distances and require exactly two distinct positive distances.
Technique and why it applies: A square has four equal side lengths and two equal diagonals, so the six pairwise squared distances form two nonzero values. Squaring avoids square roots and preserves distance comparisons.
Invariant: lookup contains the set of all pairwise squared distances among the four points.
Edge cases: The zero check rejects duplicate points. For four points, exactly two distinct nonzero distances imply the expected four-side/two-diagonal pattern under the Euclidean metric.
Complexity: Exactly six distance calculations and a fixed-size set operation give O(1) time and O(1) space, matching the labels.

Task and constraints: Find the longest harmonious subsequence, whose maximum and minimum values differ by exactly one.
Idea: Count occurrences of each value and combine counts for neighboring integer values.
Technique and why it applies: A harmonious subsequence can include all copies of x and x+1, so their frequency sum is a candidate length. The code checks neighboring keys and updates res with those combined counts.
Invariant: counter stores the frequencies of values, and res tracks the best adjacent-value frequency sum found.
Edge cases: The entire implementation is enclosed in a triple-quoted string, so it is not executable Python code as provided and defines no Solution class. If uncommented, it also references Counter without importing it in active code.
Complexity: The intended approach is O(n) expected time and O(u) frequency-map space for u distinct values, but the supplied file's quoted code does not run.

Task and constraints: Return the length of the longest subsequence whose maximum and minimum differ by one.
Idea: Count values as they are scanned and combine the current frequency with already-seen neighboring-value frequencies.
Technique and why it applies: For each num, lookup[num] is incremented; if num-1 or num+1 has appeared, their counts form a harmonious candidate. The maximum candidate is retained.
Invariant: lookup holds frequencies from the processed prefix and result is the longest harmonious subsequence found so far.
Edge cases: Arrays with fewer than two distinct adjacent values return zero. Updating online still discovers each neighboring pair when the later value is encountered.
Complexity: Each element performs a constant number of expected dictionary operations, giving O(n) time and O(u) space for u distinct values.

Task and constraints: Count the cells that receive the maximum value after a list of prefix rectangle increment operations.
Idea: Return the intersection area of all operation rectangles, or the whole matrix area if there are no operations.
Technique and why it applies: Every operation increments the top-left rectangle [0,a)×[0,b). Cells in every rectangle receive all increments, and their overlap has dimensions min(a) by min(b).
Invariant: The minima of operation heights and widths describe the common overlap of all operations.
Edge cases: Empty ops returns m*n. The method assumes each operation has two entries and nonnegative dimensions as specified.
Complexity: Finding minima across ops is O(q) time and O(q) temporary space for the unpacked coordinate tuples.

Task and constraints: Find how many cells share the maximum value after all prefix rectangle operations.
Idea: Repeatedly shrink the candidate maximum rectangle to the minimum height and width among operations.
Technique and why it applies: Each operation increments a rectangle starting at the origin, so only cells covered by every operation receive the maximum number of increments. The final overlap area is m*n.
Invariant: m and n track the dimensions of the intersection of all operation rectangles processed so far.
Edge cases: With no operations, m and n remain the original matrix dimensions and the whole matrix is counted. The input operation list is not modified.
Complexity: One pass over q operations takes O(q) time and O(1) auxiliary space, matching the space label.

Task and constraints: Return restaurants common to two lists whose index sums are minimal.
Idea: Build name-to-index maps, compute the index sum for each common name, then collect all names with the minimum sum.
Technique and why it applies: The first two loops record positions. The intersection loop fills common with index sums, and two later scans determine the minimum and gather ties.
Invariant: common maps every shared restaurant to its combined index sum; minimum is the smallest such sum after the scan.
Edge cases: The method prints 1 for each common restaurant, creating unwanted debug output. If there are no common restaurants, minimum stays infinity and the result is empty.
Complexity: Map construction and intersection are O(m+n) expected time, followed by two O(c) scans; storage is O(m+n).

Task and constraints: Find common restaurants with the smallest sum of their positions in the two lists.
Idea: Map each restaurant in list1 to its index and scan list2 while tracking the best index sum.
Technique and why it applies: For a shared restaurant, j+lookup[s] is its combined index. A smaller sum replaces the result list; an equal sum appends a tie. The early break is safe once j exceeds the best sum because lookup indices are nonnegative.
Invariant: result contains all restaurants tied at min_sum among the scanned candidates.
Edge cases: No common restaurant returns an empty list. The input lists are not modified, and equal index sums preserve every tie found.
Complexity: Building lookup and scanning list2 take O(m+n) expected time and O(m) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Count integers from zero through n whose binary representations contain no consecutive ones.
Idea: Use digit DP over the binary digits with state for the previous bit, tightness to n, and leading zeros.
Technique and why it applies: The recursion chooses each permitted bit and rejects a one when the previous bit was one. Memoization caches each state by digit position and flags.
Invariant: fun(i,last,tight,leading_zeros) counts valid completions from bit position i under the accumulated prefix constraints.
Edge cases: The DP table has only 30 position slots, but n can require 31 binary digits under common constraints; this can index past the table. The memoized state array also assumes bit length matches its fixed first dimension.
Complexity: With a correct table size, there are O(log n) positions and a constant number of states/transitions per position, so intended time and space are O(log n); the supplied dimensions can fail for large n.

Task and constraints: Count values in [0,num] whose binary representation has no adjacent ones.
Idea: Precompute Fibonacci-like counts of valid bit strings, then scan num's bits from most significant to least significant.
Technique and why it applies: dp[i] counts valid bit strings of length i. When a one bit appears, all valid numbers with a zero at that position contribute dp[i]; if the previous bit was also one, the scan stops because larger prefixes would violate the rule.
Invariant: result counts valid values with a prefix already smaller than num, and prev_bit tracks whether the previous bit was one.
Edge cases: The final +1 includes num itself when valid. If num has consecutive one bits, the loop breaks after subtracting the invalid prefix case.
Complexity: The table has fixed size 32 and the bit scan is fixed-width, giving O(1) time and O(1) space under 32-bit constraints, matching labels.

Task and constraints: Determine whether at least n new flowers can be planted without placing flowers in adjacent plots.
Idea: Add empty sentinels at both ends and greedily plant whenever the current plot and its neighbors are empty.
Technique and why it applies: The scan uses neighboring occupancy to skip positions that cannot accept a flower. When all three positions are empty, it plants in the middle and advances by two to avoid adjacency.
Invariant: could_plant counts flowers planted so far and all earlier plots have been safely processed.
Edge cases: n=0 returns True without planting. The sentinels allow the first and last real plots to use the same neighbor logic as interior plots.
Complexity: The index advances monotonically through the flowerbed, giving O(n) time and O(n) space for the padded copy.

Task and constraints: Check whether n flowers can be added without any two flowers being adjacent.
Idea: Scan each empty plot and plant there whenever both neighbors, if present, are empty.
Technique and why it applies: A placement immediately marks the plot occupied, so later checks see the updated neighborhood and cannot plant adjacent flowers. The method returns as soon as n reaches zero or below.
Invariant: Every planted flower respects adjacency, and n is the number of additional flowers still needed.
Edge cases: n=0 returns True after the first iteration, but an empty flowerbed with n=0 skips the loop and returns False; this is a corner-case bug if n may be zero. The code mutates the input list.
Complexity: Each plot is inspected once, giving O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space, matching labels aside from the zero-demand corner case.

Task and constraints: Group file paths that have identical file contents from the encoded directory descriptions.
Idea: Parse each directory line into filenames and contents, then group full paths by content.
Technique and why it applies: The first space-separated token is the directory path. Each later token is split at parentheses into a filename and its content; files sharing a content key are collected, and only groups larger than one are returned.
Invariant: files[content] contains all full paths parsed so far with that exact content.
Edge cases: The parser assumes filenames and directory paths do not contain spaces, as in the input format. It extracts only the first '(' and ')' positions.
Complexity: Parsing takes O(T) time in total input length, and the content map stores O(T) characters and paths, giving O(T) space.

Task and constraints: Count triplets that can form a triangle, meaning the sum of the two smaller positive lengths exceeds the largest.
Idea: Sort lengths and use two nested indices with a monotonic third pointer to count valid largest sides.
Technique and why it applies: For fixed i and j, every k below the first index where nums[i]+nums[j] <= nums[k] forms a triangle. Since the array is sorted, k only moves forward as j increases.
Invariant: k is the first index not satisfying the triangle inequality for the current i,j pair, so k-j-1 valid choices are counted.
Edge cases: Zero-length values are skipped as the smallest side. Sorting mutates nums; the two-pointer counting assumes nonnegative lengths and sorted order.
Complexity: The outer and middle loops are O(n²), while k advances monotonically, yielding O(n²) time and O(1) explicit auxiliary space aside from sorting temporaries.
